Introduction to QualCoder

Setting up a project, coding interview transcripts and running reports in a free qualitative analysis program

Author

NC State University Libraries — Data Science Services

Published

November 6, 2026

Open this guide anywhere: go.ncsu.edu/dss-intro-qualcoder

ImportantHow to use this guide

This is the page we work from in the session. Every step is written out, so you can follow along, catch up if you fall behind, and come back to it later.

  • Steps are in purple boxes titled with where you do them: In your browser, In Finder (Mac), In File Explorer (Windows) or In QualCoder. Everything outside a box explains what the steps do.
  • Mac and Windows steps are in tabs. Where the two differ, pick your system’s tab once and every tab on the page switches to match.
  • This guide is for QualCoder version 3.8.2. There is a version 4.0, but it is very new and some of its menus have changed.

Welcome

What you’ll be able to do

  • Install QualCoder and set up a project folder that keeps your data and backups safe.
  • Create a QualCoder project and import interview transcripts into it.
  • Code transcripts, and add memos and annotations as you go.
  • Run reports of your coded text and memos to start your analysis.

Roadmap for today

  1. See where we’re headed. We start with a look at a finished project, below.
  2. Set up a project folder on your computer and download today’s transcripts into it (Section 1).
  3. Install QualCoder (Section 2).
  4. Create a QualCoder project, set your coder name and turn on backups (Section 3).
  5. Import transcripts and describe them with attributes (Section 4).
  6. Code: watch a short demo, then code a transcript yourself for 5 minutes (Section 5).
  7. Run reports of coded text and memos (Section 6).
  8. Close the project, then reopen it to find your first backup (Section 7).

More things to try, including how to work on a project with a team, are in Extra activities.

What we’re not doing today

  • We’re not using QualCoder’s AI features. QualCoder can connect to AI tools, but sending research data to an AI service has IRB implications. Always check with your advisor and your IRB protocol before turning them on.
  • We’re not covering how to do qualitative research. Today is about the software: how to set up a project and use QualCoder’s tools.

Where we’re headed

By the end of the session you’ll have a project that looks like this: three interviews with singers, coded with a few codes (each has its own color), a memo or two, and a report that pulls together everything you coded in the interviews.

Screenshot: images/roadmap-end-result.png. The Coding tab of a finished workshop project: the codes list on the left with 2–5 codes in their colors, a transcript on the right with several passages highlighted, at least one passage underlined (2+ codes) and one italicized (memo).

Screenshot: images/roadmap-end-report.png. A report of all the codes in all three transcripts, with memos included. (Take both after the demo transcripts have been coded.)

1 Set up your project folder

Before you install QualCoder, decide where your project will live and make a folder for it. A QualCoder project is a folder ending in .qda that holds a database of your codes, memos and copies of your files. Keeping it in a folder of its own, next to your original data and your backups, makes the project easy to find, copy and hand on.

WarningGotcha: don’t use cloud storage for the project folder

Don’t put the project folder in OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, Box or iCloud. QualCoder keeps its database open while you work, and a sync program copying it at the same time can damage it or create conflicting copies.

Watch out for folders that sync without you noticing: on a Mac, Desktop and Documents may be synced to iCloud; on Windows, they may be synced to OneDrive. Your home folder is usually a safe place. Back up by copying the closed project somewhere else, not by syncing it.

You’ll make a folder called qualcoder-workshop with two folders inside it: data, for your original interview files, and backups, for QualCoder’s automatic backups. Later, QualCoder adds the project itself, intro-qc-workshop.qda, next to them (Section 3).

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn Finder: make the project folders
  1. Open Finder and go to your home folder: Go > Home (or Cmd + Shift + H).
  2. Make a new folder (File > New Folder, or Cmd + Shift + N) and name it qualcoder-workshop.
  3. Open qualcoder-workshop and make two folders inside it: data and backups.
NoteIn File Explorer: make the project folders
  1. Open File Explorer and go to your user folder: C:\Users\<your name>. (Not Documents or Desktop, which may sync to OneDrive.)
  2. Make a new folder (New > Folder, or Ctrl + Shift + N) and name it qualcoder-workshop.
  3. Open qualcoder-workshop and make two folders inside it: data and backups.

1.1 Get today’s transcripts

Today we’ll code three interviews with singers, from the Library of Congress. Each was done when one of the singer’s recordings was added to the National Recording Registry, and each singer answers similar questions: where the songs came from, how the record got made and why it still connects with people. That overlap makes them good for coding: the same ideas come up in all three, in different words.

Singer Recording Interview Length
Dolly Parton “Coat of Many Colors” (1971) 2016 about 850 words
Cyndi Lauper She’s So Unusual (1983) 2019 about 1,600 words
Alicia Keys Songs in A Minor (2001) 2022 about 2,350 words

Our research question for today: How do singers describe where their songs come from, and why those songs connect with people? A real study would start from a question like this; we use it to decide what to code.

These three come from the Library of Congress’s index of Recording Registry interviews, which has interviews with more than 100 other musicians, producers and songwriters, as PDFs.

NoteIn your browser: download the interviews
  1. Click each link to download the interview as a text file:
    • DollyParton.txt
    • CyndiLauper.txt
    • AliciaKeys.txt
  2. If a file opens in your browser instead of downloading, go back, then right-click the link (on a Mac, Control-click) and choose Download Linked File or Save link as.
  3. Move the three files from your Downloads folder into qualcoder-workshop/data.

The Library of Congress shares the interviews as PDFs, and they weren’t made for analysis: every line ends in a line break, even mid-sentence, and the interviewer is labeled “LOC”, “Library of Congress” or “LC”. For today, we’ve made plain-text copies with only the formatting tidied: each paragraph is joined back together, and the speakers are always labeled “Library of Congress:” and the singer’s name. The words are unchanged, including the editors’ notes in [square brackets].

Ideally, transcripts are clean like this before you import them: speaker labels consistent, typos fixed, and names and identifying details removed if the participants were promised confidentiality. QualCoder imports plain text (.txt), Word (.docx) and PDF files.

TipExtra: who owns an interview?

The interviews are copyrighted by their authors. The Library of Congress’s license lets it allow noncommercial scholarly and educational reuse, and it gave us permission to share these text copies for this workshop. Each file starts with a note saying so. When you reuse someone else’s interviews in your research, check the license and the terms of use first.

2 Install QualCoder

QualCoder is free, open-source software for qualitative data analysis. It runs on your own computer, so your data stays with you. If you installed it before the session, check that it opens and skip ahead to Section 3.

WarningGotcha: the newest QualCoder is 4.0, but we use 3.8.2

QualCoder 4.0 came out in October 2026, so QualCoder’s website now offers 4.0, and its menus differ from this guide. Use the download links below to get 3.8.2.

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn your browser and Finder: install on a Mac
  1. Download QualCoder_3_8_2_macOs_arm64.dmg (547 MB).
  2. Open the downloaded file from your Downloads folder.
  3. Drag QualCoder into your Applications folder.
  4. Open QualCoder from Applications. If your Mac says it can’t check the app for malicious software, go to System Settings > Privacy & Security, scroll down and click Open Anyway confirm the exact message and steps.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/install-downloads-mac.png. The downloaded .dmg file in the Downloads folder.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/install-applications-mac.png. The window that opens from the .dmg, showing QualCoder and the Applications folder (dragging QualCoder into Applications).

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/install-open-anyway-mac.png. System Settings > Privacy & Security with the Open Anyway button boxed (only if this message appears).

WarningGotcha: 3.8.2 is for Apple silicon Macs only

The 3.8.2 Mac download runs only on Macs with Apple silicon (M1 or later). To check yours, open the Apple menu > About This Mac: it lists a Chip (Apple M1, M2, …) or a Processor (Intel). There’s no Intel version of 3.8.2; the most recent Intel Mac version is 3.7 (QualCoder.3.7.Mac.X86.dmg), and some menus may differ from this guide.

NoteIn your browser and File Explorer: install on Windows
  1. Download QualCoder_3_8_2_Win_setup.exe (246 MB).
  2. Find the setup wizard in your Downloads folder and double-click it to start.
  3. When asked, choose Download only for me confirm the exact wording. On university computers you can’t install it for all users.
  4. Click through the rest of the wizard: list each button, such as Next, Install and Finish.
  5. Let the setup wizard open QualCoder when the installation is complete.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/install-only-for-me-win.png. The setup wizard step with “only for me” selected.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/install-wizard-1-win.png, install-wizard-2-win.png, … One for each later step of the setup wizard, with the button to click boxed, ending with the last screen (Finish, with the option to open QualCoder).

2.1 The first time QualCoder opens

NoteIn QualCoder: the first time it opens
  1. Wait. QualCoder is not very quick to open.
  2. When it asks whether you want to set up AI, click No. You can always set it up later.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/install-ai-prompt.png. The AI setup question QualCoder shows on first launch, with No boxed.

3 Create a QualCoder project

3.1 Menus and tabs

QualCoder has two ways to get around, and this guide uses both:

  • The top menu: Project, Manage, Coding, Reports, AI and Help. On a Mac, it’s in the menu bar at the top of the screen, after the Qualcoder menu. On Windows, it’s at the top of the QualCoder window.
  • The tabs inside the QualCoder window: Action Log, Manage, Coding, Reports and AI Chat. Choosing an item from the top menu often opens one of these tabs.

Screenshot: images/project-menus-tabs.png. The top of the QualCoder window with the top menu and the tabs each boxed and labeled, so the two are easy to tell apart.

3.2 Create the project

  • Mac
  • Windows

NoteIn QualCoder: create a new project
  1. Go to Project > Create New Project (or Cmd + N).
  2. In the save window, go to your qualcoder-workshop folder.
  3. Name the project intro-qc-workshop and click Save. QualCoder adds .qda to the name.
  4. The project opens right away in QualCoder.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/project-create-mac.png. The Mac save window, inside qualcoder-workshop, with the name intro-qc-workshop typed in. It’s an ordinary save window, so the steps are enough on both systems.

NoteIn QualCoder: create a new project
  1. Go to Project > Create New Project (or Ctrl + N).
  2. In the save window, go to your qualcoder-workshop folder.
  3. Name the project intro-qc-workshop and click Save. QualCoder adds .qda to the name.
  4. The project opens right away in QualCoder.

Suggest skipping (to discuss with Nina): images/project-create-win.png. The Windows save window, inside qualcoder-workshop, with the name intro-qc-workshop typed in. It’s an ordinary save window, so the steps are enough on both systems.

3.3 Set your coder name

QualCoder records who coded each passage. Set your name now, so your codes are labeled with it. This is especially important when you check coding between coders or team members, to make sure codes are applied consistently.

The settings are in a different menu on each system.

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn QualCoder: open the settings
  1. Go to Qualcoder > Preferences… (or Cmd + ,). On a Mac, the settings are in the Qualcoder menu, not the Project menu.
NoteIn QualCoder: open the settings
  1. Go to Project > Settings (or Alt + S).

The Settings window and the coder list are the same on both systems.

NoteIn QualCoder: set your coder name
  1. Next to Current coder, click Change.
  2. Click New, type your coder name and click OK.
  3. Make sure your coder name has a check mark next to it.
  4. Click OK.

Screenshot: images/project-coder-name.png. The coder list with a new name added and its check mark (either system).

3.4 Turn on backups to your backups folder

QualCoder can keep backups of your project for you. Point it at the backups folder you made.

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn QualCoder: set the backup folder
  1. Go to Qualcoder > Preferences… (or Cmd + ,).
  2. Click Default project directory.
  3. Go to qualcoder-workshop and click once on backups to select it (don’t double-click into it).
  4. Click Open.
  5. Click OK.
NoteIn QualCoder: set the backup folder
  1. Go to Project > Settings (or Alt + S).
  2. Click Default project directory.
  3. Go to qualcoder-workshop and click once on backups to select it (don’t double-click into it).
  4. Click Select Folder.
  5. Click OK.

Screenshot: images/project-backups-win.png. The Windows folder picker with backups selected and Select Folder boxed.

QualCoder makes a backup each time you open the project and keeps up to 5 backups in this folder. When it saves a new one, it deletes the oldest. Backups are folders named like intro-qc-workshop_BKUP_<date>_<hour>.qda. Your first one appears the next time you open the project; you’ll see it at the end of the session (Section 7).

3.5 Confirm your settings

When you click OK to close the settings, QualCoder reports the project settings and any changes in the Action Log tab. It updates every time you change the project.

NoteIn QualCoder: check the Action Log
  1. Click the Action Log tab.
  2. Check that your coder name and the project directory are right.

Screenshot: images/project-action-log.png. The Action Log tab after the settings change, showing the coder name and directory.

4 Import transcripts

4.1 Import the files

QualCoder copies each file into the project. Later edits in QualCoder change only that copy; your original in data/ stays as it was.

NoteIn QualCoder: import transcripts
  1. In the top menu, click Manage > Manage Files. This opens the Manage tab.
  2. Click the Import file into project folder button.
  3. QualCoder opens its own Open file window. Go to the data folder inside qualcoder-workshop.
  4. Select all three transcripts: click the first, then hold Shift and click the last.
  5. Click Open.

4.2 Add attributes

Attributes describe your files: for example, the participant’s role, the interview date or the site. They help you keep track of which file is which, and you can use them to filter reports.

We’ll add two attributes to the interviews: the singer’s Genre (text) and the Year of the recording (a number).

File Genre Year
DollyParton.txt Country 1971
CyndiLauper.txt Pop 1983
AliciaKeys.txt R&B 2001
NoteIn QualCoder: create two attributes
  1. In the top menu, go to Manage > Manage Attributes.
  2. Click the (x) button to add an attribute.
  3. Type Genre, choose Character (text), and choose Files for what it describes (it can also describe cases or journals). Click OK.
  4. Click (x) again. Type Year, choose Numeric and Files, and click OK.

Screenshot: images/attributes-create.png. The new attribute window with a name typed, the type chosen and Files selected.

NoteIn QualCoder: fill in the attribute for each file
  1. Click Manage > Manage Files. Each attribute is now a column.
  2. Click the cell for each file and type its value from the table above. To edit a value, double-click the cell.

Screenshot: images/attributes-values.png. The Manage tab with the attribute column filled in for each transcript.

TipExtra: put attributes in your own order

QualCoder lists attributes alphabetically. To set your own order, number them: “1. Year”, “2. Genre”.

5 Code your transcripts

5.1 Get ready to code

NoteIn QualCoder: open a transcript for coding
  1. In the top menu, click Coding > Code Text. This opens the Coding tab.
  2. Check that it shows your name as the coder. If it doesn’t, click the … box next to the coder name and choose your name. (If your name isn’t there, add it in the settings: see Section 3.)
  3. Click the name of the transcript you want to code. Its text appears in the large box on the right.

Screenshot: images/coding-ready.png. The Coding tab with the coder name boxed, the file list on the left and a transcript open on the right.

5.2 Demo: coding with example codes

Watch first, then try it. We’ll code part of the Cyndi Lauper interview together, with four example codes that fit our research question. Each code has a short definition, so everyone (and your future self) applies it the same way.

Code Use it when the singer… Where to look, for example
Inspiration from life ties a song to something that happened to them or people they know Cyndi Lauper on the loud clock behind “Time After Time”
Industry pushback describes the record company, managers or radio disagreeing with them, or them pushing back Cyndi Lauper on choosing her first single
Faith and spirituality mentions God, faith or a spiritual feeling Alicia Keys on the chorus of “Troubles”
Why it connects explains why listeners relate to the song Dolly Parton on why “Coat” became so dear to people

A list of codes like this, with definitions and examples, is a codebook. In your own research you’d build and revise it as you read.

Highlight the text you want to code, then use a keyboard shortcut or right-click:

To do this Shortcut Or right-click and choose
Code with a new code Shift + N Mark with new code (N)
Code with a recently used code Shift + R Mark with recent code (R), then pick from the list
Remove a code from text Shift + U Unmark (U)

The shortcuts are the same on Mac and Windows confirm on a Mac.

NoteIn QualCoder: code a passage
  1. Open CyndiLauper.txt.
  2. Highlight her answer about where “Time After Time” came from (the clock and the watch).
  3. Press Shift + N, type Inspiration from life and click OK. The passage is highlighted in the code’s color, and the code appears in the codes list on the lower left.
  4. Add the other three codes the same way, each on a passage that fits it.
  5. Highlight another passage that fits a code you’ve already made, press Shift + R and pick the code from the list.
  6. To remove a code, click in the coded text and press Shift + U.

Screenshot: images/coding-new-code.png. A highlighted passage with the right-click menu open, Mark with new code (N) boxed.

Right-click in the codes list to rename a code, change its color, add a memo to it, add a new code or category, or delete it.

5.3 Do it yourself: 5 minutes of coding

NoteIn QualCoder: your turn (5 minutes)
  1. Open DollyParton.txt. It’s the shortest of the three.
  2. Read it and code passages with the four example codes. If you’d like to, add one code of your own.
  3. Try coding one passage with two codes, so it’s underlined.
  4. Pick a passage you’ve coded and add a memo to it (see the next section).
  5. Finished early? Code some of the Alicia Keys interview, so your reports have more to show.

5.4 Memos

A memo is a note attached to coded text. After you code a passage, add a memo that sums it up: what about this text helps answer your research question? For example, on a passage coded Inspiration from life: “Turns a painful memory into a song; writing it helped her let go of the hurt.” Later you can run a report of only memos (Section 6), which gives you a head start on writing your analysis.

NoteIn QualCoder: memo coded text
  1. Code the text first.
  2. Click anywhere in the coded text.
  3. Press Shift + M, or right-click and choose Memo coded text (M).
  4. Type your memo and close the window. The memo’d text is now italicized.

If the text has more than one code, QualCoder asks which code the memo belongs to. That choice decides where the memo shows up in reports.

Screenshot: images/memos-coded-text.png. The memo window open on a coded passage.

5.5 Annotations

An annotation explains a piece of text: an acronym, short-hand or a reference a reader wouldn’t know. Unlike a memo, the text doesn’t need to be coded. For example, Dolly Parton mentions “Porter”: an annotation can say that’s Porter Wagoner, the country singer she performed with at the time.

NoteIn QualCoder: annotate text
  1. Highlight the text that needs explaining.
  2. Press Shift + A, or right-click and choose Annotate (A).
  3. Type the annotation. The annotated text is now bold.

Screenshot: images/annotations.png. An annotation window open on “Porter” in the Dolly Parton interview.

5.6 What the formatting means

What you see What it means
Highlighted and underlined The text has 2 or more codes.
Highlighted and italicized A memo is attached to the coded text.
Bold An annotation is attached to the text.

In the codes list (lower left of the Coding tab), drag codes to merge them, move them into a category or reorder them. In the color picker, colors marked with an asterisk (*) are already used by a code; hover over one to see which.

6 Run reports

A report pulls together all the text for the codes and files you choose. We’ll start with everything: all the codes in all three interviews. Then we’ll add memos to the report.

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn QualCoder: report all your coded text
  1. In the top menu, click Reports > Coding reports confirm the menu path.
  2. Select all three transcripts: click the first, then hold Shift and click the last. (To pick only some, hold Cmd and click each one.)
  3. Select all the codes, the same way.
  4. Leave the memo drop-down at None.
  5. Click the large Play button at the top.

Screenshot: images/reports-coded-text-mac.png. The report window with files and codes selected and the Play button boxed.

NoteIn QualCoder: report all your coded text
  1. In the top menu, click Reports > Coding reports confirm the menu path.
  2. Select all three transcripts: click the first, then hold Shift and click the last. (To pick only some, hold Ctrl and click each one.)
  3. Select all the codes, the same way.
  4. Leave the memo drop-down at None.
  5. Click the large Play button at the top.

Screenshot: images/reports-coded-text-win.png. The report window with files and codes selected and the Play button boxed.

6.1 Include memos, or only memos

The memo drop-down (it says None to start) decides whether memos are in the report. There are two kinds of memo: memos on coded text, like the summaries you wrote today, and memos on codes themselves (right-click a code, View or edit memo), which work like a codebook to remind you what each code means.

Choose The report shows
None All the coded text, no memos.
Also code memos All the coded text, plus the memos on your codes.
Also coded memos All the coded text, plus the memos on coded text: the summaries that give you a head start on analysis.
Also all memos All the coded text, plus both kinds of memo.
Only memos Both kinds of memo, and no coded text.
Only coded memos Only the memos on coded text, and no coded text.
NoteIn QualCoder: add your memos to the report
  1. Keep all the transcripts and codes selected.
  2. In the memo drop-down, choose Also coded memos.
  3. Click Play. Your memos now appear with the text they’re attached to.
NoteIn QualCoder: report only your memos
  1. In the memo drop-down, choose Only coded memos.
  2. Click Play. The report now lists just your memos: a first draft of your analysis notes.

6.2 A codes-by-file matrix

A matrix shows which codes appear in which files: codes are columns and files are rows.

NoteIn QualCoder: make a matrix
  1. Keep all the transcripts and codes selected, and set the memo drop-down back to None.
  2. In the drop-down next to the Play button, choose Codes by file.
  3. Click Play. To swap rows and columns, check Transpose matrix.

Screenshot: images/reports-matrix.png. A codes-by-file matrix for today’s transcripts.

6.3 Try other reports

To get a different report, change what’s selected and click Play again.

Screenshot: images/reports-options.png. The whole report window with each setting boxed and labeled: the file list, the code list, the memo drop-down, the matrix drop-down and the Play button.

QualCoder has many other report formats and settings. See the QualCoder reports documentation.

7 Close your project

WarningGotcha: always close the project when you’re done

Close the project whenever you’re done for the day. An open project is locked, so if it’s on a shared computer or a shared drive, nobody else can open it until you close it. Closing also makes sure everything is saved before you copy the folder anywhere.

7.1 Close the project

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn QualCoder: close the project
  1. Go to Project > Close Project (or Option + X).
  2. Click the Action Log tab. It lists what changed in this session and ends with Closing project.

Screenshot: images/close-project-mac.png. The Project menu on a Mac with Close Project boxed.

NoteIn QualCoder: close the project
  1. Go to Project > Close Project (or Alt + X).
  2. Click the Action Log tab. It lists what changed in this session and ends with Closing project.

7.2 Reopen the project and find your backup

QualCoder makes a backup when you open a project, so reopening it now creates your first backup in the backups folder.

NoteIn QualCoder: reopen the project
  1. Go to Project > Open Recent Project and choose intro-qc-workshop.qda.
  2. Click the Action Log tab. Look for Project backup created, followed by the backup’s location in qualcoder-workshop/backups and its name, such as intro-qc-workshop_BKUP_20261106_10.qda (the date and the hour).

Screenshot: images/close-backup-log.png. The Action Log after reopening the project, with the Project backup created line boxed. Crop it so no username shows in the path.

7.3 Close it again and quit

  • Mac
  • Windows
NoteIn QualCoder: close the project and quit
  1. Go to Project > Close Project (or Option + X).
  2. Quit QualCoder: Qualcoder > Quit Qualcoder (or Cmd + Q).
NoteIn QualCoder: close the project and exit
  1. Go to Project > Close Project (or Alt + X).
  2. Exit QualCoder: Project > Exit (or Ctrl + Q).

Extra activities

These are in the QualCoder Quick Start guide but not in today’s session. Try them on the workshop project, or come back to them when you start your own.

Working as a team

A QualCoder project can’t be opened by two people at once, so decide how you’ll work together before you create the project.

Working one at a time (sequentially). Only one person works on the project at any moment. Either:

  • Do all the coding on one computer, used by one person at a time, or
  • Code on several computers and pass the project on: close it, zip the .qda folder and send it to the next person.

Working at the same time (in parallel). Each person has their own project folder.

  • The transcripts imported into each project can be exactly the same, or each person can take a share.
  • Ideally, agree on the codes before you start. It’s fine if you don’t, but then documenting your codes is extra important.
  • You can share project folders with each other when you want to.

Either way, agree as a team on where project files will live and how to name each person’s project folder. If the team has several deliverables, a subfolder per deliverable helps. Set a different coder name for each person (Section 3), and keep a shared list of which color goes with which code.

To see what one person coded, run a report (Section 6) and choose their name from the Coder drop-down at the top left of the report window.

Open an existing project

QualCoder may open your most recent project when it starts. If it doesn’t:

NoteIn QualCoder: open a project
  1. Click Project > Open Project, go to your project folder, click once on the .qda folder and click Select Folder (Mac: button name).
  2. Or click Project > Open Recent Project and choose the project.

Each time you open QualCoder, check that you’re in the right project.

Fix a typo in a transcript

If you spot an error in a transcript (for example, “force plan” where the speaker said “forest plan”), you can fix it in QualCoder.

NoteIn QualCoder: edit transcript text
  1. In the Coding tab, click the Edit Text button. Text that’s already coded is underlined.
  2. Make your changes. Keep edits small: single words, short phrases or punctuation.
  3. Click End Edit Text when you’re done.

The change is made only in the project’s copy of the transcript; the original file isn’t changed. For anything bigger, clean the file (in Word, for example) before you import it.

Memo a whole file

Use a file memo to track progress, such as “Coded, 10/1/26”.

NoteIn QualCoder: add a file memo
  1. Go to Manage > Manage Files.
  2. Click once in the Memo column for the file and type your memo.

More coding shortcuts

New code Quick code Recent code Uncode
Shift + N Shift + Q Shift + R Shift + U
Add memo Annotate Mark important Bookmark
Shift + M Shift + A Shift + I Shift + B
  • Quick code (Shift + Q) applies the same code you used last.
  • Shift + ← and Shift + → extend coded text to the left or right. QualCoder can be slow at this; it’s often quicker to uncode and recode the passage.
  • The color picker has options for color vision deficiencies.

Code other kinds of files

QualCoder can code PDFs, images, audio and video, not just text. See Coding text and the rest of the documentation.

QualCoder’s AI features

QualCoder can work with AI tools to help search and code your data. Before you turn this on, check with your advisor and your IRB: sending research data to an AI service may not be allowed under your protocol. See the QualCoder documentation.
